title: Stationary Points and Critical Points
quickIdea: Stationary means f'(c) = 0. Critical means f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist. Every stationary point is critical; not every critical point is stationary.
remember: c is a stationary point of f if f is differentiable at c and f'(c) = 0 - the tangent there is horizontal.
c is a critical point if f'(c) = 0 or f is not differentiable at c.
Stationary subset of critical. A corner or a vertical tangent gives a critical point that is not stationary, as at 0 for |x|.
Extrema can occur only at critical points (Fermat's theorem for the differentiable case, plus the non-differentiable case), so the critical points are the complete candidate list.
A critical point is only a candidate: x^3 at 0 is stationary and is neither a maximum nor a minimum.

example.prompt: List the critical points of f(x) = |x| and of g(x) = x^3, and say which are stationary.
example.work: For f, f'(x) = 1 for x > 0 and -1 for x < 0, and f'(0) does not exist, so 0 is critical and not stationary. For g, g'(x) = 3x^2, which vanishes only at 0, so 0 is stationary and therefore critical.
example.answer: f has one critical point, 0, which is not stationary. g has one critical point, 0, which is stationary. Neither function's critical point set contains anything else.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2026 Set 1 Q.36 asks directly about a function built from |x|: it asks whether f has a local maximum, whether f has a local minimum, whether f' is continuous, and whether f' is not differentiable. All four statements are about where the derivative exists and where it vanishes, which is the stationary/critical distinction applied twice.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many critical points does f(x) = x^(2/3) have, and how many are stationary?
variations.answer: One critical point, at x = 0, and none of them is stationary: f'(x) = (2/3) x^(-1/3) is never zero and fails to exist at 0.
variations.why: The same distinction on a cusp instead of a corner. The count of critical points does not change; the reason it is critical does.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is every point where f' = 0 a critical point? Is every critical point a point where f' = 0?
variations.answer: Yes to the first, no to the second.
variations.why: The containment is one-way, and both directions appear as distractors in statement-style questions.

trap.what: Using 'critical point' to mean only the solutions of f'(x) = 0, so that points where the derivative fails to exist are dropped from the candidate list.
trap.why: Extrema do occur at non-differentiable points - |x| at 0 is the standard example - so dropping them can lose the answer.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = |x| has its only minimum at 0, where f' does not exist. Solving f'(x) = 0 gives no candidates at all.

check.question: f(x) = x^4. How many stationary points does f have, and how many critical points?
check.answer: One stationary point, at x = 0, and one critical point, the same one.
check.explanation: f'(x) = 4x^3 exists everywhere and vanishes only at 0, so there are no critical points of the non-differentiable kind.
